cases.quote: In principle, small kana (cl-11) should be placed neither at the head of a line nor that of an inline cutting note in principle. If it were to be allowed, HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL * shall be treated as part of the hiragana (cl-15) class, and KATAKANA LETTER SMALL * as part of the katakana (cl-16) class.
cases.rationale: U+3041 is the first row of §A.11, and §A.11 is a heading and a five-column table with nothing else in it: no preamble sentence, no note, no cross-reference. Its Remarks cell is empty, as all forty-one are in both renderings, so the section qualifies no member by frame (字幅), by writing direction or by role, and membership is the whole of what it states. What an occurrence answers is not membership alone, because the document states four times — §3.9.2's third cl-11 note, §B.2 note 16, §C.2 note 3 and §E.2 note 3 — that a small kana permitted at a line head is treated as a member of hiragana (cl-15) or katakana (cl-16). §C.3 grants that permission at three of its four levels, and the third is headed "Strict (Default, general publications)" / 「レベル3（デフォルト，一般の書籍）」. spec/derived/questions.tsv records kinsoku.level jlreq = strict and kinsoku.relaxation_mechanism jlreq = reclassify, so an implementation declaring Policy::JLREQ is scored against the second entry below rather than the first: the empty overlay is the fallback, and the applying entry naming the most questions is the one selected. The English half quoted above carries "in principle" twice in one sentence, where the parallel note for cl-10 says it once; it is quoted as published. Its Japanese half asserts what the English half omits — 「ただし，小書きの仮名（cl-11）を行頭又は割注行頭に配置することを許容する処理方法もあり，書籍などでもよく採用されている」, that the permissive method exists and is often adopted in books — which is the evidence for the default this case turns on, and it is stated in one rendering only.

forbidden.why: The reclassification does not have one target. §B.2 note 16 keys it on the UCS name — "HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL * shall be treated as part of the hiragana (cl-15) class, and KATAKANA LETTER SMALL * as part of the katakana (cl-16) class" — and §C.2 note 3 keys it on "the script type of the character". U+3041 is HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL A and its script is Hiragana, so it is treated as cl-15 under either formulation and never as cl-16. An implementation that sends the whole class to katakana answers twenty-nine of §A.11's forty-one rows correctly and the other twelve wrongly.

cases.rationale: The last row of §A.11 and the only key in cl-11 that is not a single code point. Three facts meet in it. Its first code point U+31F7 is also listed alone, as the thirty-second of the forty-one rows, so the key can be found only by matching longest-first — an implementation scanning code point by code point finds the short key and stops. Its second code point U+309A is listed nowhere in Appendix A, under any class, so an implementation that splits the pair reports two occurrences where the document has one and the second of them is unlisted. And §C.2 note 3 states the reclassification in terms of "the script type of the character", which for this key is the Katakana of U+31F7: U+309A is Script=Inherited and carries no script of its own. §B.2 note 16's formulation cannot reach this row at all, because it names the two targets by the UCS names KATAKANA LETTER SMALL * and HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL * and this key's name is a pair name, so the script clause is what decides it — which is why §B.2#16 is not among the rules this case exercises and the other cl-11 cases carry it. This case supplies the pair as one item and can therefore assert only the answer to the joined key: a case states its own items, so an implementation that would have split the pair is not observable here, and what catches it is the input contract rather than an expectation.

Every one of its forty-one Remarks cells is empty in both renderings, so the section draws no width distinction of the kind §A.13 draws with "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」 or §A.1 with "used in horizontal composition" / 「横組で使用」; and no key of cl-11 is named by any other Appendix A table, which is unusual, since two Appendix A keys in five are named by more than one class. cases.quote: For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: §A's preamble scopes every one of its tables to a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 — collections 285 and 286 — and its Note says what real Japanese text carries instead: the compatibility counterpart of the code point the table keys. cl-11 has nine of them, U+FF67 through U+FF6F, whose UnicodeData.txt decompositions are <narrow> onto U+30A1, U+30A3, U+30A5, U+30A7, U+30A9, U+30E3, U+30E5, U+30E7 and U+30C3 — the five small katakana vowels, ャ, ュ, ョ and this one. The decomposition tag is itself a statement about width, so a caller who set U+FF6F has thereby declared the half-em frame and this item says so; a full-em declaration on the same code point would be a diagnostic rather than a silent choice. The folding is the Wide and Narrow decompositions and nothing wider, because full compatibility folding would fold U+2160 onto "I" and lose a genuine §A.19 member. The class does not move with the frame here: §A.11's Remarks column states no width, and no other Appendix A table lists U+30C3, so the same answer is due on every frame.

cases.rationale: The example row §3.9.2 prints for cl-11, supplied as the eighteen occurrences it is, with the case asking about the eleventh — HIRAGANA LETTER SMALL TU, the sokuon (促音). All eighteen are in §A.11's table, so the example and the enumeration agree here, which is not true of every class in this document. The sokuon is where the glossary's two halves part: §G defines the class in English as "Kana with smaller letter faces to be used mainly for representing contracted sounds or prolonged vowels. (JIS Z 8125)" and in Japanese as 「拗音，促音，外来語などを書き表す場合に用いる，字面を小さくした仮名．捨て仮名，半音ともいう．（JIS Z 8125）」. 拗音 is the contracted sound the English half names; 促音 is this character, and the English half does not name it; and the "prolonged vowels" the English half puts in its place are written with U+30FC, which is cl-10 and not in this class at all. The divergence is not recorded in spec/derived/defects.tsv. The stream is also the negative statement about keys: cl-11 holds exactly one code-point sequence, it is <31F7, 309A>, and it is not in this string, so eighteen characters are eighteen occurrences and nothing joins.

cases.rationale: The document states one permission twice, in two forms that are not equivalent, and this case records both readings and the choice that selects each. §C.3 states it as an override of Table 2 — the sentence quoted above, under the level heading "Strict (Default, general publications)", followed by a list naming 々, cl-10 and cl-11 — which changes a break decision and names no class for the occurrence to become. §C.2 note 3, §B.2 note 16 and §E.2 note 3 state it as a change of class, and note 3 adds the dereference instruction "(For how it behaves in combination with other character classes, see the cells for hiragana (cl-15) or katakana (cl-16).)", which reaches every cell of the row and the column rather than the line-head cell alone. The two readings differ for an occurrence in the middle of a line, where one changes the spacing and the adjustment opportunities and the other does not, so this is not a distinction without a difference. spec/derived/questions.tsv records kinsoku.relaxation_mechanism as contradictory with jlreq = reclassify, so this project takes the second reading and the empty overlay below carries the first. cases.quote: In vertical writing mode, the letter face of small kana (cl-11) characters (ぁぃぅァィゥ etc.) is placed at the vertical center and to the right of the horizontal center of the character frame; in horizontal writing mode, it is placed at the horizontal center and below the vertical center (see Figure 4).
cases.rationale: cl-11 is named twice among the document's vertical-and-horizontal differences, and neither mention makes membership conditional on a direction. The sentence quoted above places the letter face (字面) inside the character frame, and §3.1.1 restates it in the section that enumerates those differences, where cl-06 and cl-07 are named for the same reason and cl-01, cl-02 and cl-03 are named for a rotation. A letter face inside a frame is the caller's font: the character frame is the same em in both directions, the class is the same class, and nothing here reads the direction to answer it. §A.11's Remarks column says so from the other side — all forty-one cells are empty, where §A.1 qualifies U+2018 and U+201C with "used in horizontal composition" / 「横組で使用」, which is what a direction-restricted member looks like when the document states one. This case therefore declares no direction and must answer identically composed either way. U+30F6 is the member most likely to raise the question by another route, since it is set as an abbreviation for 箇 in 三ヶ月; §A.11 gives it no qualification, and cl-11 has no role axis at all.

cases.rationale: This is the boundary of cl-11, and it is the one an English-only reader crosses. §G's entry for the class reads, in English, "Kana with smaller letter faces to be used mainly for representing contracted sounds or prolonged vowels. (JIS Z 8125)" — but a prolonged vowel in Japanese is written with U+30FC, which §A.10 lists as the sole member of the prolonged sound mark (cl-10) and which §A.11 does not list at all. The Japanese half of the same entry says 拗音，促音，外来語 and never says 長音, so the English half attributes cl-10's job to cl-11 in the one place a reader looks for a definition rather than an enumeration. The divergence is not recorded in spec/derived/defects.tsv. §3.9.2's own first note on cl-11 says why the two are separate classes here at all: JIS X 4051's "Japanese characters with no line break allowed before" is divided in this document into iteration marks (cl-09), prolonged sound mark (cl-10) and small kana (cl-11). The three permitted answers below are cl-10's own and take the same shape as this file's, because §C.2 note 2 sends a relaxed prolonged sound mark to katakana (cl-16) exactly as note 3 sends small kana to hiragana or katakana, and §C.3 relaxes cl-10 and cl-11 side by side at each of its three relaxing levels.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: U+1B155 KATAKANA LETTER SMALL KO is a small katakana by its UCS name and by its script — Scripts.txt gives 1B155 to Katakana — and §A.11 does not list it. Nine such code points are in the vendored UnicodeData.txt and in none of Appendix A's tables: U+1B132, U+1B150 through U+1B152, U+1B155, and U+1B164 through U+1B167, all encoded after this document's tables were written. §A's preamble is what draws the line, because it scopes the lists to ISO/IEC 10646 collections 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION", and the sentence quoted above records that the handling of a character the lists do not mention is implementation-defined and that this document inherits that position. So an answer here is a published reading and never a requirement, which is why this case's standing is unstated and both readings are recorded. The trap is specific to this class: §C.2 note 3 requires a script lookup over exactly the ranges that contain this code point, so an implementation that already reads Scripts.txt for the reclassification has everything it needs to answer cl-11 here, and must not. A name test fails the same way, since the UCS name of this code point contains SMALL and so does the name of every member of the class.
